dishes.name: Sweet and Sour Carp
dishes.description: Yellow River carp fried golden with tail raised high, draped in an amber sweet-and-sour sauce. The skin cracks like thin ice; within, the flesh is tender and snow-white. Sour leads into sweet, sweetness never overwhelming freshness, with a glossy glaze clinging to the plate—the definitive taste of New Year in old Jinan memory.
dishes.history: Rooted in traditional Yellow River carp cookery, Jinan's Huiquan Lou famously fried live carp to order in the late Qing. Shandong sweet-sour technique demands 'fry first, then glaze.' The dish crystallized in the Republican era as the signature of Yanxi Tang and Jufeng De, witnessing Jinan's port-city banquet splendor.
dishes.method:
Score carp in peony-cut pattern, marinate with salt and Shaoxing wine 15 min
Coat with starch batter, hold tail, lower into 70% hot oil; fry until set, then re-fry for crispness
Separately stir-fry scallion, ginger, garlic; make sauce with sugar-to-vinegar 2:1
Thicken with wet starch, add hot oil to brighten and bubble the glaze
Pour sauce over fish immediately and serve sizzling hot
dishes.eatingGuide: Key line: Eat the back crust first, then dip in the bottom glaze. Take a piece with skin; crisp yields to tender, tongue meets vinegar aroma, sugar sweetness, then fish savor. Pair with white rice, mixing glaze through it—the old Jinan way. Cold halves the pleasure, so eat piping hot.
dishes.culturalCode: Key line: Carp leaps the dragon gate; the table holds heaven and earth. This dish carries the fish veneration of Yellow River farming culture, its glaze symbolizing prosperity. On Jinan banquet tables, the whole fish faces the guest of honor with tail intact, meaning surplus year after year—a regional etiquette of taste.
dishes.honestTalk: Many places now swap common carp for Yellow River carp—the texture gap is huge. For the authentic version, reserve at a time-honored restaurant. Tourist-zone fast-food versions are basically sweet-sour fried fish slices; don't expect much.

dishes.name: Braised Intestines in Nine Turns
dishes.description: Intestines pass through blanching, boiling, layering, and braising; the result is date-red, glossy, shaped in looping coils. Texture is soft-sticky yet springy: first sour, then sweet, then salty, finishing with light bitterness and spice—five flavors rotating on the tongue in rich sauce, revealing the true meaning of 'nine turns'.
dishes.history: In the Guangxu era of Qing, Manager Du of Jinan's Jiuhua Lou, who loved intestines, created this dish. Named from the Daodejing's 'Nine-Turn Golden Elixir'—the process as intricate as refining immortality pills. Later refined by Lu cuisine masters, it became famed north-south as official cuisine; during the Republic, Peking opera stars always ordered it when visiting Ji'nan.
dishes.method:
Rub pork intestines with salt and vinegar to remove odor; blanch, then boil with scallion and ginger until 80% cooked
Layer intestines (two or three tubes nested) for thickness; cut into sections
Stir-fry over medium heat until both sides turn golden and slightly charred
Add Shaoxing wine, soy sauce, sugar, clear stock, amomum powder, cinnamon powder; simmer 20 min over low heat
Reduce over high heat, drizzle with Sichuan pepper oil, flip, and plate in chrysanthemum shape
dishes.eatingGuide: Key line: One bite, five flavors surging like waves. Don't swallow whole—bite across the cross-section, first tasting the sweet-salty outer glaze, then chewing the fragrant inner layers. Pair one piece with a small sip of hot tea to cut richness; best alongside semi-dry yellow wine or Jinan's Baotu Spring beer for full effect.
dishes.culturalCode: Key line: Coarse materials, fine craft—Confucian merchant virtue. Nine-Turn Intestines embodies Jinan official cuisine's philosophy of 'transforming the ordinary into the magical.' Turning offal into perfection typifies Lu cuisine's grandeur, restraint, and refined technique, mirroring Jinani pride in craftsmanship and propriety.
dishes.honestTalk: This dish lives or dies by skill; one missed step brings rankness or grease. Street-corner versions tend to be cloyingly sweet without acid, or mushy without chew. For real mastery, try upscale restaurants—ask if the chef uses amomum powder first; if not, skip it.

dishes.name: Cattail Shoots in Milk Broth
dishes.description: Tender hearts of Daming Lake cattail shoots simmered in milk-white broth, thick and mellow as fresh cream. Shoots are translucent, crisp, and fiber-free, with a clean sweetness that echoes. The soup tastes rich yet light, lifted by ham and shiitake—one spoonful seems to drink the essence of a spring itself, a unique vegetarian treasure of the spring city.
dishes.history: Cattail shoots rank among Jinan's 'Three Beauties' (with lotus root and water caltrop). Records of eating bulrush shoots appear in the Northern Wei's Qimin Yaoshu. Qing-era Jinan milk broth, made from hen, pork hock, and duck carcass, met cattail shoots to become an official banquet classic, perfected at Jinsheng Lou, with literati praising it 'clear as autumn dew.'
dishes.method:
Remove hard husk from cattail shoots; take tender core and slice; shred ham, shiitake, and bamboo shoots
Simmer hen, pork hock, and duck bones at least 3 hours; strain for pure stock
Bring stock to boil; add shoots, ham, shiitake; simmer 2 min over low heat
Season with salt, Shaoxing wine, ginger juice; no soy sauce to keep soup white
Finish with chicken fat or lard; ladle into bowl, scatter pea shoots on top
dishes.eatingGuide: Key line: Sip the broth first, then eat the core, scrape the last gleam from the bowl. As soon as it arrives, take a spoonful of the soup, letting richness and sweetness wash over you. Then pick up a shoot—hardly chew, just feel its crisp tenderness dissolve. When soup's gone, dip half a bun in what's left; don't waste the creamy essence.
dishes.culturalCode: Key line: Spring-fed nourishment; clean and pure conduct. Milk Broth Cattail Shoots is the taste symbol of Jinan's 'spring city culture'—the dish pure white, the broth jade-like, signifying the scholar-official's integrity. Using the humblest ingredient to reach ultimate flavor reflects Qilu aesthetics of naturalness and quiet endurance.
dishes.honestTalk: True cattail shoots peak only from April to June; other seasons bring celtuce or young lotus root imposters—texture is worlds apart. And proper milk broth needs half a day of real ingredients; many joints cheat with cow's milk—one sip tastes greasy and fishy, and that's not Jinan.

dishes.name: West Lake Vinegar Fish
dishes.description: Grass carp or mandarin fish is scalded to seven-tenths doneness, then glazed with amber sweet-sour vinegar sauce. The flesh is as tender as tofu, opening with sour notes and finishing sweet, carrying a subtle crab-like aroma with ginger to cut fishiness. Its color is glossy red-brown.
dishes.history: Originating from the Southern Song capital Lin'an legend of 'Sister Song's Fish Soup,' it evolved into a famed Qing-dynasty restaurant dish. Named for keeping fish in West Lake water to remove muddy taste, it is a living history on Hangzhou's tables.
dishes.method:
Slaughter live fish, scale, split along spine into two halves, rinse clean
Boil water with scallion, ginger, and Shaoxing wine; cook fish skin-side up for 3 minutes until just done
Drain and plate, reserve 250ml cooking liquid
Season liquid with soy sauce, sugar, and rice vinegar; thicken with wet starch to a glossy glaze
Pour over fish and sprinkle with minced ginger and white pepper
dishes.eatingGuide: Eat hot, or it turns fishy. Pick a belly piece, dip in glaze, and pair with plain rice—sour opens appetite, sweet lingers. Don't pick out ginger; mix it in to cut richness.
dishes.culturalCode: In sweet-sour lies Jiangnan's elegance. This dish balances 'fish freshness, vinegar tang, sugar sweetness' like Hangzhou's character—outwardly gentle, inwardly refined, not fierce or bland—a plate-level emblem of Song culture's golden mean.
dishes.honestTalk: Truth: first-timers often find the vinegar sharp, but with rice it grows addictive. Choose mandarin fish if possible—fewer bones, finer flesh, far friendlier than grass carp.

dishes.name: Longjing Shrimp
dishes.description: Fresh river shrimp are coated and flash-fried to snowy white, then tossed with tender Longjing tea leaves picked before Qingming. Tea fragrance seeps into the meat, which is bouncy and clean, with a faint bitter-sweet finish. No oily sheen on the plate—refined as an ink painting.
dishes.history: Inspired in late Qing by Hangzhou chefs exploring 'tea banquets,' it used Hupao spring water to steep Longjing leaves, cooking shrimp with the brew. Set in the 1930s at Louwailou, it became a literati-cuisine icon.
dishes.method:
Shell live river shrimp, wash with salt and egg white until white, coat with starch, chill 2 hours
Steep fresh Longjing in 80°C water; drain broth, reserve a few leaves
Heat wok, cold oil, slide shrimp until color changes, remove and drain
Keep base oil, add tea broth and shrimp, stir-fry quickly, add thin starch slurry
Scatter tea leaves, toss once, plate immediately
dishes.eatingGuide: One bite, spring never forgotten. Eat plain—skip vinegar dips so tea and shrimp sweetness meet on your tongue; follow with a sip of warm Longjing for a longer finish.
dishes.culturalCode: If tea never enters meals, how can one know Jiangnan? Longjing Shrimp elevates daily tea-drinking into poetry on a plate, honoring natural rhythms—spring tea meets spring shrimp, season as cosmic order—this is literati gastronomy.
dishes.honestTalk: Honest take: it looks simple but demands master technique. Restaurants often charge over 100 yuan; homemade versions tend to toughen or fishy taste—splurge at an old brand for genuine value.

dishes.name: Dongpo Pork
dishes.description: A whole slab of skin-on pork belly cut into 4cm cubes, slow-simmered in Shaoxing wine for two hours. Skin turns date-red and translucent, fat melts instantly, lean stays tender without shredding. Soy and wine aromas interlace, sweet-savory balanced, sauce thick as glue.
dishes.history: Attributed to Northern Song poet Su Shi, when as Hangzhou governor he rewarded workers dredging West Lake: he braised donated pork in yellow wine, teaching 'slow fire, little water.' Named Dongpo Pork, it thrives a millennium on.
dishes.method:
Blanch pork belly to set shape, cut into cubes, score skin crosswise
Line clay pot with scallion and ginger; place pork skin-side down
Add light soy, dark soy, rock sugar, and Shaoxing wine to cover
Boil high, then simmer on micro-flame 90 minutes
Flip skin-side up, simmer 30 more minutes, reduce sauce to glossy finish
dishes.eatingGuide: One piece, three bowls of rice—worth the trip. Pick up a trembling cube with chopsticks, melt the fatty skin first, then chew lean meat; spoon sauce over rice. Skip cold drinks to avoid heaviness.
dishes.culturalCode: Fire time done right, skill follows. Dongpo Pork is about 'slowness' and 'patience,' echoing Su Shi's resilience through exile—no rush, simmer bitter days into sweet tenderness. It is Hangzhou's wisdom of enduring calmly.
dishes.honestTalk: Sounds too fatty? Prolonged braising renders out most oil, so it's not greasy at all. But watch portions if you're health-conscious: a half piece as a taste, then pack the rest home—it's even better tossed with noodles.

dishes.name: Mapo Tofu
dishes.description: Silken tofu simmered in a rich, fiery sauce of fermented broad beans, chili oil, and Sichuan peppercorns. Invented in the late Qing Dynasty by Chen Mapo, a restaurateur in Chengdu. The dish balances the signature "mala" (numbing-spicy) flavor with the delicate softness of tofu.
dishes.history: Originated in the late Qing Dynasty (c. 1860s) at Chen Xingsheng Restaurant in Chengdu. The owner's wife, Chen Mapo, created this dish. It was inscribed as a national intangible cultural heritage dish in 2010.
dishes.method:
1. Cube silken tofu, blanch briefly.
2. Fry ground beef in chili oil until crisp.
3. Add doubanjiang (fermented bean paste), garlic, ginger.
4. Add tofu and stock, simmer gently.
5. Thicken with cornstarch slurry.
6. Finish with ground Sichuan peppercorn oil.
dishes.eatingGuide: Scoop it over rice, 1:1 ratio. Mapo Tofu is a sauce-delivery system — the silky tofu and red oil are designed to coat every grain of steamed rice. Don't eat it alone; it's too intense. Start with small bites; the numbness builds up with each spoonful. The layer of red oil on top is normal — mix it in, don't skim it off.
dishes.culturalCode: Why it matters beyond taste: Mapo Tofu is the ultimate test of a Sichuan chef — it looks simple but requires perfect control of 7-8 seasonings working in harmony. It embodies the "hundred dishes, hundred flavors" (百菜百味) philosophy of Sichuan cuisine: even a dirt-cheap ingredient like tofu can become legendary with the right technique. In 2010, it became one of the first dishes inscribed on China's national intangible cultural heritage food list.
dishes.honestTalk: Real mapo tofu is much oilier than what you get abroad. That crimson oil slick on top? It's supposed to be there. Western versions are often watered down to be "healthier," which misses the point entirely. One bowl of rice with mapo tofu is one of the most satisfying meals you can have for under $3 in Chengdu. Warning: it stains clothes permanently — wear dark colors.

dishes.name: Kung Pao Chicken
dishes.description: Diced chicken stir-fried with peanuts, dried red chilies, and scallions in a sweet-savory sauce. Named after Ding Baozhen, a Qing Dynasty official whose title was "Gongbao".
dishes.history: Named after Ding Baozhen (1820–1886), a Qing Dynasty governor of Sichuan who loved this dish. It spread globally and is one of the most recognized Chinese dishes internationally.
dishes.method:
1. Marinate diced chicken in soy sauce and cornstarch.
2. Prepare sauce: vinegar, soy sauce, sugar, cornstarch, water.
3. Flash-fry chilies and peanuts.
4. Stir-fry chicken until white.
5. Combine all with sauce, toss until glossy.
dishes.eatingGuide: Eat it immediately — it waits for no one. Kung Pao Chicken loses its "wok hei" (镬气, breath of the wok) within 5 minutes. The peanuts should still have a slight crunch. Pick out the dried chilies — they're for flavoring the oil, not eating whole. The ideal bite has chicken, a peanut, and a sliver of scallion all in one mouthful.
dishes.culturalCode: Why it matters beyond taste: This is the most successfully exported Sichuan dish globally, but the version you get abroad is heavily westernized — sweet, mild, almost no Sichuan peppercorns. The original has 20+ dried chilies and a numbing, not sweet, profile. Its global journey mirrors the story of Chinese immigration: from railroad workers in the 1800s to suburban takeout joints today.
dishes.honestTalk: Most foreigners have never had real Kung Pao Chicken. The American version is sweet stir-fry with a few chili flakes — a completely different dish. Real Sichuan kung pao will make your lips go numb, and that's the whole point. If you order it in Chengdu and get a thick, sweet sauce, you're in a tourist trap. The best kung pao is served at small, crowded restaurants where the chef is visible through the kitchen window.

dishes.name: Sichuan Hotpot
dishes.description: A communal dining experience centered around a pot of simmering, chili-laced broth. Diners cook raw ingredients tableside — from thin-sliced beef to tripe, lotus root, and tofu skin.
dishes.history: Roots trace to Jialing River boatmen of the Ming/Qing era who cooked offal in spicy broth. Modern Sichuan hotpot emerged in Chongqing in the early 1900s and spread nationwide by the 1990s.
dishes.method:
1. Prepare broth: beef tallow, chili, Sichuan pepper, fermented beans, spices.
2. Slice ingredients thinly.
3. Bring broth to rolling boil.
4. Dip and cook ingredients briefly.
5. Dip in sesame oil with garlic and cilantro.
dishes.eatingGuide: The dipping sauce is not optional. Mix sesame oil + crushed garlic + cilantro + a spoonful of the broth. That's the classic Chengdu combo. Never dip your used chopsticks into the shared pot — use the serving chopsticks (公筷). Cooking times: tripe 15 seconds (any longer and it's rubber), beef 30 seconds, veggies 2 minutes, tofu just to warm through. Start with mild ingredients before meat to let the broth develop flavor.
dishes.culturalCode: Hotpot is the most social meal in Chinese culture. The round table, the shared bubbling pot, the chaos of everyone cooking at their own pace — it's a metaphor for Chinese family life. In Sichuan, hotpot isn't just food; it's a ritual. People don't say "let's go eat hotpot" to mean a quick meal — they mean a 2-hour bonding session with good friends and cold beer. The spicier the pot, the closer the friendship.
dishes.honestTalk: The "mild" broth at Sichuan hotpot places is still very spicy by Western standards. If you can't handle heat, order a yuanyang (鸳鸯) pot — split broth, half spicy, half clear chicken broth. The oil-based broth is NOT soup — don't drink it. The sesame oil dipping sauce isn't for flavor; it cools the spice and protects your stomach lining. Your clothes will smell like hotpot for at least two days after. Accept it. And yes, the bathroom line at a hotpot restaurant at 9 PM on a Saturday tells you everything about Chengdu's food culture.

dishes.name: Jiangyou Braised Pork Intestine
dishes.description: A legendary Sichuan dish from Jiangyou County, featuring pork intestines braised to tender perfection in a rich, spicy sauce. Chewy, bold, and definitely NOT for everyone. Dare to take the ultimate Sichuan challenge?
dishes.history: Originated in Jiangyou (modern-day Mianyang) during the Qing Dynasty, when local butchers simmered leftover pork offal with chili and spices to make a hearty, affordable meal. By the Republican era, it had grown into a beloved street food sold at market stalls. In the 1970s, state-run restaurants standardized the recipe for mass production. The 1980s saw a revival as small private eateries brought back family recipes with unique twists, cementing its status as Jiangyou's culinary icon and a Sichuan food heritage dish.
dishes.method:
1. Thoroughly clean the intestines by scrubbing with flour and salt, then rinse and blanch in boiling water.
2. In a wok, heat oil and sauté ginger, garlic, doubanjiang (fermented broad bean paste), and dried red chilies until the oil turns red and fragrant.
3. Add the intestine pieces, splash in cooking wine and soy sauce, toss in star anise and cinnamon, and stir-fry briefly.
4. Pour in enough boiling water to cover the intestines, bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer gently for 1.5 hours until fork-tender.
5. Turn up the heat and reduce the sauce until thick and glossy; garnish with fresh cilantro and scallions before serving.
dishes.eatingGuide: Chew thoroughly — this is not a delicate bite. Pork intestine is inherently bouncy. The first mouthful might surprise you; that's normal. Eat it with a big scoop of rice — the sauce is the real star here, so spoon it generously over the grains. If you're a first-timer, start by eating the sauce and rice to acclimate to the flavor profile before tackling the intestine itself.
dishes.culturalCode: This dish embodies the Chinese philosophy of "waste nothing" (物尽其用). Every part of the animal is cooked deliberately and with skill. Across China, offal dishes are a test of a chef's ability: can you transform the parts others discard into something people crave? In Sichuan, the best chefs aren't judged by how they handle premium cuts, but by how they elevate humble ingredients.
dishes.honestTalk: Pork intestine is not for everyone, and that's OK. It has a distinct mineral flavor and a texture that many Westerners find challenging — bouncy, almost rubbery, with a slight chew that takes getting used to. Even many Chinese people don't eat it. If you're trying it, commit to at least three bites; the first bite is mostly psychological. And a critical warning: if the intestine isn't cleaned perfectly (which requires serious skill), it tastes exactly like you'd imagine uncleaned intestine would taste. Go to reputable places only.

dishes.name: Husband and Wife Lung Slice (Fuqi Feipian)
dishes.description: Thin slices of beef, beef tripe, and offal in a numbing chili oil dressing. The name sounds wild — but the flavor is unforgettable. Brave hearts only.
dishes.history: Created in the 1930s by Guo Zhaohua and his wife in Chengdu. Despite the alarming name (no literal lungs are used), it became a cold dish staple across Sichuan. The name comes from the original vendors being a husband-wife team.
dishes.method:
1. Boil beef shank, tripe, and tongue until tender, chill and slice paper-thin.
2. Prepare dressing: chili oil, Sichuan peppercorn oil, soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, crushed garlic.
3. Arrange slices, drizzle dressing, top with crushed peanuts and cilantro.
4. Serve cold.
dishes.eatingGuide: Mix it thoroughly before eating. The dressing settles at the bottom — every slice needs to be coated in that red oil. The tripe with honeycomb texture is the best part. Eat it as a cold appetizer with beer. It's served at room temperature or chilled, never hot. Pro tip: at a Sichuan banquet, this dish arrives early — pace yourself, it's meant to last through several rounds of drinks.
dishes.culturalCode: This is one of the most misleadingly named dishes in Chinese cuisine. No lungs. No husband-wife requirement to eat it. The name reveals something deeper about Chinese food culture: names are often poetic, deliberately provocative, and always have a story behind them. The dish itself is a masterpiece of cold cooking — it requires no heat, just perfect knife work and seasoning ratios. In Sichuan, a chef's reputation is built on their cold dish (凉菜) skills as much as their hot wok work.
dishes.honestTalk: The name scares off more foreigners than the actual ingredients. There's nothing weird in this dish — it's essentially dressed cold cuts with Sichuan spices, no different from Italian bresaola or German cold meat platter. The "lung" is a historical translation error from the 1930s that stuck. If you've ever had deli meat, you can handle this. It's probably the safest "exotic" dish on this list to try. That said, some versions use beef tongue, which has a distinct texture — stick to the tripe and shank slices if you're cautious.

dishes.name: Rabbit Head (Tu Tou)
dishes.description: Sichuan's most controversial street snack — a whole rabbit head, spiced and braised. Intense flavor, hands-on eating. Not for the faint of heart.
dishes.history: A specialty of the "Rabbit Capital" of China — Sichuan consumes over 300 million rabbits annually. Rabbit head braised in spicy broth became a late-night street food staple in Chengdu in the 1990s.
dishes.method:
1. Clean rabbit heads thoroughly, blanch to remove impurities.
2. Braise in spiced broth (star anise, cinnamon, Sichuan pepper, dried chili, doubanjiang) for 45 minutes.
3. Let cool in broth to absorb flavor.
4. Serve with extra chili powder and Sichuan pepper on the side.
dishes.eatingGuide: You eat it with your hands. There is no polite way. Start from the cheek — the meatiest, most rewarding part. Then the tongue (a single, satisfying morsel). Then the brain (tiny, creamy, for the brave). Work around the skull piece by piece. This is not a meal; it's a process — meant to be consumed over an hour with beer, not wolfed down in five minutes. Each head yields maybe 20 grams of actual meat.
dishes.culturalCode: Why 300 million rabbits a year in Sichuan? It's not random. Sichuan's humid climate is ideal for rabbit farming, and rabbits reproduce fast. But rabbit head isn't about nutrition — it's about the act of eating itself. In Chinese food culture, there's a category called "消遣食品" (time-pass food) — dishes that take time to eat, that occupy your hands and engage your full attention. Rabbit head is the king of time-pass foods. It's social eating at its most primal.
dishes.honestTalk: This is the dish that separates adventurous eaters from the rest. The honest truth: a rabbit head has very little meat — mostly bones, cartilage, and the satisfaction of extracting tiny morsels. The flavor of the braising liquid is excellent, but the effort-to-reward ratio is debatable. Some foreigners love it for the experience; others try it once and never again. If the full head is too much, order "rabbit legs" (兔腿) instead — same flavor, way more meat, zero existential crisis. CNN reporters who tried it in Chengdu were "initially apprehensive but ultimately won over by the complex flavors."

dishes.name: Grilled Brain Flower (Kao Nao Hua)
dishes.description: Silky, creamy pig brain grilled on a skewer with chili, cumin, and Sichuan pepper. An acquired taste — but fans call it the ultimate late-night indulgence. Dare to try?
dishes.history: Emerged as a late-night street food in Chengdu in the 2000s, paired with beer and skewers. It reflects Sichuan's "eat everything" food culture and the philosophy of wasting nothing.
dishes.method:
1. Clean fresh pig brain, remove membranes, keep whole.
2. Marinate briefly in Shaoxing wine and ginger.
3. Grill on skewer over charcoal, brush with chili oil, cumin, and Sichuan pepper mix.
4. Serve hot, eat with a spoon.
dishes.eatingGuide: Eat it with a small spoon, like a custard. The texture is the whole point — silky, creamy, almost mousse-like. Don't chew; press it against the roof of your mouth to let it dissolve. It's served hot, straight off the charcoal — let it cool for 30 seconds first. Pair with a cold beer. One skewer is enough for a first try; it's surprisingly rich.
dishes.culturalCode: Brain as food spans cultures worldwide — French cervelle, Mexican sesos, Sichuan kao nao hua. In Sichuan, it follows the "eat everything" philosophy and the belief that eating organ meats nourishes corresponding organs (以形补形). What makes the Sichuan version unique is the heavy spice treatment — the chili and cumin don't just season the brain; they transform it into something that even people who "don't like the idea of eating brain" can enjoy.
dishes.honestTalk: If you're squeamish, don't look at your skewer too closely before eating. The brain retains its shape on the skewer, which puts many people off. The flavor, however, is surprisingly mild — much milder than you'd expect. It mostly tastes like the spices it's grilled with. The texture is the real challenge: if you can handle silken tofu, you can handle brain. But if you're not sure, split one skewer with a friend first. And yes, grilled brain is genuinely delicious — there's a reason it's survived as street food for two decades.

dishes.name: Dan Dan Noodles
dishes.description: Chengdu's iconic street noodles — thin wheat noodles topped with a spicy, numbing sauce of preserved vegetables, chili oil, Sichuan peppercorns, and minced pork. Originally carried by pole-bearing street vendors (dan dan).
dishes.history: Originated in the early 20th century in Chengdu. Vendors carried noodles and stove on a shoulder pole (dan dan) and stopped to cook a bowl for passersby. It became a UNESCO-recognized intangible cultural heritage dish in 2024.
dishes.method:
1. Make sauce base: chili oil, Sichuan peppercorn powder, soy sauce, black vinegar, sugar, minced garlic.
2. Cook thin noodles, drain, place in bowl.
3. Top with sauce, minced pork stir-fried with ya cai (preserved vegetable), cilantro, peanut powder.
4. Mix thoroughly before eating.
dishes.eatingGuide: Mix it fast and thoroughly. The sauce is at the bottom and the noodles will clump if you wait. Every strand needs to be coated. Eat it immediately — standing at the stall is part of the experience if that's how it's served. The portion is intentionally small; it's a snack (小吃), not a main course. In Chengdu, people order 2-3 bowls in one sitting if they're hungry.
dishes.culturalCode: One of the few Chinese dishes recognized by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage (2024). The "dan dan" carrying pole method — one basket for noodles, one for the stove — shows the ingenuity of Chinese street vendors who turned a simple survival job into culinary art. Today the shoulder pole is gone, but the dish remains as a direct connection to Chengdu's street food past. It's fast food, Chinese style: made in 2 minutes, eaten in 5, remembered for a lifetime.
dishes.honestTalk: Most dan dan noodles outside Sichuan are wrong. The real version is dry (no soup) with a thick, clinging sauce. That soupy version you see in Western Chinese restaurants? It's a mutation that doesn't exist in Chengdu. The key ingredient that makes it authentic is "芽菜" (ya cai, preserved Sichuan vegetable) — it's almost impossible to find outside China, which is why the abroad version never tastes right. When in Chengdu, order it at a street stall, watch the vendor mix it by hand, and eat it within 60 seconds of serving.

dishes.name: Sliced Fish in Hot Chili Oil (Shui Zhu Yu)
dishes.description: Tender fish fillets poached in mild broth, then smothered in hot chili oil with dried chilies and Sichuan peppercorns. The oil is for aroma, not for drinking — scoop it aside and enjoy the fish.
dishes.history: A modern Sichuan classic from the 1980s, created by chef Fan Jun in Chongqing. It revolutionized "fish cooking" in Sichuan cuisine, combining the numbing-spicy flavor with delicate white fish.
dishes.method:
1. Marinate fish fillets (carp or catfish) in egg white and cornstarch.
2. Poach fillets gently in light broth, transfer to serving bowl.
3. Top with dried chilies, Sichuan peppercorns, garlic, scallions.
4. Pour smoking-hot oil over toppings to release aroma. Serve immediately.
dishes.eatingGuide: Fish first, then the vegetables, then leave the oil. The top layer of chili oil is for aroma and heat insulation — scoop it aside, don't eat through it. The fish should be incredibly tender; if it's rubbery, it's been overcooked. Save a spoonful of that chili-flake-laced oil to drizzle over your rice — it's a bonus meal in itself.
dishes.culturalCode: Shui Zhu Yu is a modern Sichuan classic — only about 40 years old. Before the 1980s, fish in Sichuan was always cooked with less aggressive seasonings. Chef Fan Jun's innovation broke that tradition completely. The dish symbolizes the evolution of Sichuan cuisine in modern China: unafraid to break rules, bold in execution, and purely focused on flavor delivery. It's also the textbook example of the Sichuan principle "油而不腻" (oily but not greasy) — the oil carries flavor but doesn't feel heavy when done right.
dishes.honestTalk: The amount of oil is shocking, even by Chinese standards. A proper shui zhu yu has a 2cm layer of chili oil floating on top. That's normal, not a mistake. The good news: the fish itself is not spicy — the spice is all in the oil layer and the dried chilies on top. So if you're nervous, gently push the top oil aside and scoop fish from underneath. Warning: whole Sichuan peppercorns hide in the oil like little flavor grenades — one surprise bite can ruin the next 30 seconds. Chew carefully.

dishes.name: Kaishui Baicai (Boiled Cabbage in Supreme Broth)
dishes.description: Perhaps the most deceptive dish in all of Sichuan cuisine. What looks like plain cabbage in clear water is actually the pinnacle of Sichuan's clear-soup technique — a masterwork that shatters the stereotype that Sichuan is only about spice. Tender cabbage hearts bathed in a crystal-clear, impossibly flavorful broth made from hours of careful preparation.
dishes.history: Created in the late Qing Dynasty by legendary Sichuan chef Huang Jinglin. At a time when Sichuan cuisine was dominated by bold flavors, Huang wanted to demonstrate its versatility. Drawing inspiration from imperial court cooking techniques, he developed this elegantly clear dish. It was so well-received that it entered the imperial palace kitchens. Later refined by generations of master chefs, it became a signature dish on China's state banquet menus — served to visiting foreign dignitaries.
dishes.method:
1. Prepare the "supreme broth": combine old hen chicken, old duck, pork ribs, Jinhua ham, and dried scallops. Simmer on low heat for 6+ hours to create a rich base stock.
2. Pound chicken breast and lean pork into a fine paste (meat "velvet").
3. Slowly stir portions of the meat velvet into the warm stock — it attracts and absorbs fats and impurities. Repeat and strain several times until the broth is completely clear, resembling plain water.
4. Select only the pale yellow innermost leaves of napa cabbage. Trim, blanch briefly, then plunge into ice water to lock in color and crunch.
5. Arrange cabbage hearts in a porcelain bowl, pour in the hot clear broth, steam for 10 minutes until the cabbage absorbs the soup's essence.
dishes.eatingGuide: Drink the broth first, then eat the cabbage. Don't add anything — no salt, no chili, nothing. The entire point of this dish is purity. Take a spoonful of the "clear water" — you'll be shocked by the depth of flavor. It's savory, complex, and lingers on the palate without any heaviness. Then the cabbage: crisp, sweet, soaked in the essence of the broth. Pro tip: the temperature matters — it should be served piping hot. If it's lukewarm, the magic diminishes significantly.
dishes.culturalCode: This dish single-handedly proves that Sichuan is more than just "mala" (numbing-spicy). The "one dish, one style; a hundred dishes, a hundred flavors" philosophy of Sichuan cuisine is often lost on outsiders who think everything is covered in chili oil. Kaishui Baicai represents the yin to mala's yang — restraint after excess, clarity after intensity. It's also a story of chefs pushing boundaries: Huang Jinglin created it to prove that Sichuan chefs could master the most refined imperial techniques, not just street-level robust flavors.
dishes.honestTalk: The honest truth: This dish is almost impossible to find outside of high-end banquet settings. The broth takes 6+ hours of active attention and the meat-velvet clarification technique is labor-intensive. Most "kaishui baicai" you'll encounter in ordinary Chengdu restaurants is a simplified version — good, but not the real thing. If you want to taste the authentic version, you need to go to a top-tier Sichuan restaurant or a state banquet. And yes, it looks like a bowl of hot water with cabbage — that's the whole point. The deception is the art.

dishes.name: San Da Pao (Three Cannons — Chengdu's Loudest Snack)
dishes.description: A performance disguised as a snack. Three sticky glutinous rice balls are thrown with force against a wooden board fitted with brass plates — producing three explosive "BANG — BANG — BANG" sounds like cannon fire. The rice balls bounce into a tray of toasted soybean flour, are rolled in the powder, then served with brown sugar syrup and sesame. It's the only Chinese snack that announces its own arrival.
dishes.history: Originated about 100 years ago (1910-1920s) at the Qingyang Palace Flower Fair, Chengdu's largest temple fair. The creator was a street vendor named Li Hongxing who sold sticky rice cakes. Competition was fierce, so he devised a gimmick: he threw three rice balls at a wooden board fitted with brass discs, producing three loud "clangs" — named Iron Cannon, Artillery Cannon, and Rifle Cannon. The noise drew huge crowds and made his stall famous overnight. It was named one of Chengdu's Top Snacks in 1990 and listed as a Chengdu Intangible Cultural Heritage item in 2010.
dishes.method:
1. Soak round glutinous rice in cold water for 12+ hours until it crushes easily between fingers.
2. Steam rice for 30-40 minutes on cheesecloth, sprinkling boiling water twice to prevent dryness.
3. Pound hot steamed rice with a wooden mallet for 10-15 minutes until sticky, stretchy, with slight grain texture remaining.
4. Roast soybeans until fragrant and golden, grind into fine powder.
5. Prepare brown sugar syrup: brown sugar + water, simmer until thick and glossy.
6. To serve: set up the board with brass plates facing the soybean flour tray. Tear off three uniform balls from the hot rice cake. Throw each one forcefully at the brass plates — three bangs. The balls ricochet into the soybean flour, coating evenly.
dishes.eatingGuide: Eat it immediately while warm. The sequence: pick up a soybean-coated rice ball (it's hot, be careful), dip it in the brown sugar syrup, take a bite. The outer layer is nutty and dry from the soybean flour; the inside is soft, warm, and chewy; the syrup adds caramel sweetness. The perfect pairing: a cup of bitter aged tea (老荫茶 or 老鹰茶) — the bitterness cuts the sweetness perfectly. The three balls are meant to be eaten one after another, not shared — this is a snack of indulgence.
dishes.culturalCode: San Da Pao is the ultimate example of "auditory marketing" in Chinese street food. Before digital advertising, street vendors needed creative ways to stand out. Li Hongxing's "three cannons" was pure genius — everyone within 200 meters heard the bangs and came running. It represents the carnival spirit of Qingyang Palace Fair, the biggest temple fair in western Sichuan. Along with Zhang's Cold Noodles and Sugar Oil Fruits, it was known as one of the "Three Kings of Fair Snacks." The snack is inseparable from the fair experience — eating it elsewhere is just not the same.
dishes.honestTalk: The honest truth: San Da Pao is more about the experience than the taste. The rice ball itself is simply glutinous rice — not particularly flavorful. The magic is in the auditory performance, the fresh soybean flour, and the nostalgia. If you judge it purely on flavor, it's just sweet sticky rice. But if you judge it on the whole package — the bang, the scent of roasted soy, the warm chewiness, the brown sugar — it's unforgettable. Look for it at temple fairs or traditional snack streets in Chengdu, not fancy restaurants. And don't expect it to travel well — it needs to be eaten within minutes of being "fired."

dishes.name: Leshan Sweet Glazed Duck (Tianpi Ya)
dishes.description: A whole duck brined with Sichuan spices, air-dried, brushed with maltose syrup, then deep-fried until the skin transforms into a glossy, caramelized amber. The crackling-sweet exterior gives way to tender, spice-infused meat — a perfect balance of sweet and savory that defines Leshan's culinary identity.
dishes.history: Originated in Leshan, Sichuan during the Qing Dynasty, inspired by traditional "Zhangcha Duck" smoking techniques. Local chefs replaced the smoking step with maltose glazing and deep-frying, creating a uniquely crispy-sweet skin. Today it is Leshan's most famous dish — locals say "a trip to Leshan without Sweet Glazed Duck is no trip at all."
dishes.method:
1. Clean duck, marinate overnight with salt, Sichuan pepper, ginger, star anise.
2. Blanch briefly in boiling water, air-dry 4-6 hours until skin tightens.
3. Brush evenly with maltose syrup.
4. Deep-fry in 160°C oil, basting constantly until skin turns golden-amber and crisp.
5. Drain, chop into bite-sized pieces, serve warm.
dishes.eatingGuide: How to eat it: Sweet Glazed Duck is typically served as a cold appetizer — it's already fully cooked and delicious at room temperature. Pick up a piece with your fingers (yes, it's finger food!) or chopsticks. The ideal bite has crispy skin + tender meat + a touch of the rendered fat. Pro tip: ask for the "leg quarter" (tui) if you want the meatiest pieces, or the "wing section" (chi) for max crispy skin. The skin loses its crunch within 2 hours of cooking, so eat it fresh. Many locals save the carcass to make a broth the next day.
dishes.culturalCode: Why this dish matters beyond taste: Leshan sits at the confluence of the Min, Dadu, and Qingyi Rivers — historically one of Sichuan's busiest inland ports. The abundance of ducks (river trade byproduct) and sugar (Sichuan was a major cane sugar producer) created the perfect conditions for this dish. Unlike Peking Duck (an imperial court dish served with delicate pancakes), Tianpi Ya is a "people's duck" — born from riverside ingenuity, not palace kitchens. The use of maltose glazing instead of smoking reflects Sichuan's culinary philosophy: bold, unapologetic flavors served without ceremony.
dishes.honestTalk: The honest truth: Sweet Glazed Duck is spectacular when fresh, but mediocre after sitting too long. If you buy it as takeaway and eat it 2+ hours later, the skin will be soft and chewy, not crispy — you'll wonder what the hype is about. Also, it's genuinely rich: half a duck feeds two people easily. Some Western tourists find it "too sweet for a savory dish" — if that sounds like you, order it with a side of fresh vegetables or a cold beer to cut through the richness. And the best place to eat it? Not a restaurant — look for the small shops with ducks hanging in the window, frying fresh batches throughout the day.

dishes.name: Bobo Chicken
dishes.description: Cold skewers of chicken, tripe, duck tongue, lotus root, and vegetables steeped in a chilled broth of chili oil, Sichuan pepper, sesame, and aromatics. "Bobo" means earthenware pot in Sichuan dialect — the vessel that holds this intensely flavored, numbing-spicy cold treat.
dishes.history: Dating to the Qing Dynasty in Leshan, created by a chef surnamed Bo. Unlike Chengdu's hot skewers, Bobo Chicken is served cold — the longer the skewers steep, the deeper the flavor penetrates. A beloved street snack, sold from bamboo baskets by roadside vendors carrying signature ceramic pots.
dishes.method:
1. Poach whole chicken in ginger-scallion water until just cooked.
2. Prepare chilled broth: chicken stock, chili oil, ground Sichuan pepper, sesame paste, garlic, sugar, five-spice powder.
3. Cool broth completely and refrigerate.
4. Skewer chicken pieces, tripe, duck tongue, lotus root, potato slices.
5. Submerge skewers in cold broth for at least 1 hour before serving.
dishes.eatingGuide: How to eat it: Bobo Chicken is served cold — don't ask them to heat it up! Pick a skewer, slide the food off with your teeth (or chopsticks), and dip it in the extra chili-sesame sauce bowl if provided. The magic is in the steep time: skewers that have been sitting for 2+ hours taste dramatically better than fresh ones. Pro tip: order it early in your meal and let it sit while you eat other dishes. The bamboo skewers are reusable — street vendors often collect and wash them.
dishes.culturalCode: Why this dish matters beyond taste: Bobo Chicken embodies Sichuan's "cold-eating" tradition, a lesser-known counterpart to the famous hotpot culture. In Sichuan's humid summers, cold dishes like bobo chicken offer a refreshing escape from oppressive heat — no need to hover over a boiling pot. The "bobo" (earthenware pot) itself is key: clay keeps the broth cool naturally, a pre-refrigeration innovation. This dish also reveals Sichuan's hierarchical snack culture — from humble bamboo-basket street vendors to upscale restaurants serving "premium bobo" with abalone and sea cucumber.
dishes.honestTalk: The honest truth: Bobo Chicken can be shockingly spicy for first-timers. The cold broth carries the heat differently than hot soup — it sneaks up on you. If you have low spice tolerance, ask for "wei la" (微辣, mild spicy). Also, hygiene varies wildly at street stalls — go for busy ones with high turnover. The tripe and duck tongue can be chewy and texturally challenging; stick to chicken, lotus root, and potato slices if you're new to offal. And a local secret: the best bobo chicken isn't sold in restaurants — it's the grandmother who sets up a single pot on a street corner at dusk and sells out in 2 hours.

dishes.name: Leshan Qiaojiao Beef (Crossed-Leg Beef Soup)
dishes.description: A soul-warming beef offal soup simmered with over 30 Chinese medicinal herbs. Clear golden broth, tender sliced beef and tripe, with a subtle aromatic complexity from white peony root, amomum villosum, and other traditional herbs. Light yet deeply flavorful — Leshan's most iconic comfort food.
dishes.history: Originated in Suji Ancient Town, Leshan during the Guangxu reign of the Qing Dynasty (over 100 years ago). Suji was a salt transport dock where boatmen and porters worked in damp, cold conditions. A local traditional Chinese medicine doctor began boiling beef bones and offal with 30+ medicinal herbs (white peony, amomum, etc.) to create a warming soup, given free to workers. Diners would cross one leg over the other on the crude wooden stools — hence the name "Crossed-Leg Beef."
dishes.method:
1. Split beef bones, blanch, and simmer for hours until broth is clear and rich.
2. Clean beef, liver, tripe and other offal; boil and slice thin.
3. Add herbal pouch (white peony, amomum, and 30+ herbs) to the simmering broth.
4. To serve: place sliced offal in a bowl, pour boiling broth over twice to warm and remove any smell, then add fresh broth.
5. Serve with a dipping dish of crushed chili, ground Sichuan pepper, and cilantro.
dishes.eatingGuide: How to eat it: The authentic way is "bowl-by-bowl scalding" (wan wan tang) — each bowl is individually assembled. The clear broth lets the natural flavors shine. Take a sip of the herbal broth first — it's warm, soothing, and complex. Then dip the beef and tripe in the dry chili mix. The tripe should be crunchy, the beef tender, and the broth fragrant with medicinal herbs. Pro tip: the best part is the last mouthful of broth — all the flavors from the dipped meats have enriched it. Don't skip the dipping mix (干碟) — it's not complete without it.
dishes.culturalCode: Why this dish matters beyond taste: Qiaojiao Beef is a living artifact of Leshan's salt-trade history. Suji Ancient Town was once one of the busiest salt ports on the Min River, and this dish was born from the intersection of labor, poverty, and traditional Chinese medicine. The "free soup for workers" origin makes it one of the few Chinese dishes with a genuinely charitable backstory. Its designation as Sichuan's "Intangible Cultural Heritage" recognizes not just the recipe, but the social history it represents — a dish that feeds both body and spirit.
dishes.honestTalk: The honest truth: This is not a dish for people who don't eat offal. The traditional version uses beef tripe, liver, tongue, and other innards — if that's not your thing, some shops offer a "pure beef" version (纯牛肉). The herbal flavor can be subtle or strong depending on the shop; if you're unfamiliar with Chinese medicinal herbs, start with a small bowl. And the "crossed-leg" dining posture is real — low wooden stools force you to sit with one leg up, which locals say aids digestion. The best Qiaojiao Beef in Leshan is in Suji Ancient Town, where the original recipe is still followed.

dishes.name: Linjiang Shredded Eel
dishes.description: Fresh稻田 eels from Leshan's rice paddies, skillfully deboned with an ox-bone knife into perfect shreds, then quick-fried in pork fat with pickled chilies, Sichuan pepper, and local herbs. The eel shreds are silky and bouncy, coated in a complex sauce that balances spiciness with fragrant acidity. A representative of Leshan's "fresh-spicy" cooking style.
dishes.history: Originated in Pingxing Town (formerly Linjiang Town), Leshan during the late Qing Dynasty — over 100 years of history. Legend has it that an elderly local needed eel for medicinal purposes; his family deboned the eel with an ox-bone knife and cooked it with pickled chilies and Sichuan pepper, accidentally creating this fragrant delicacy. In 2021, it was officially listed as a Leshan Intangible Cultural Heritage item — the dish that locals reserve as the grand finale for important guests.
dishes.method:
1. Select live yellow eels (3-5 qian weight) from rice paddies; keep in clean water to purge.
2. Boil eels for 3-5 minutes until 70% cooked.
3. Use an ox-bone knife to make three cuts, deboning into even shreds while preserving the tender muscle texture.
4. Fry pickled ginger, pickled chilies, and pickled mustard greens in pork fat until fragrant.
5. Add the eel's own cooking broth, eel shreds, patchouli (huoxiang), and Chinese toon (xiangchun).
6. High-heat quick-stir until the sauce coats every shred.
dishes.eatingGuide: How to eat it in three steps: First, slurp the eel shreds — silky, bouncy, each strand coated in the spicy-sour sauce. Second, crunch the crispy fried eel bones — dusted with flour and deep-fried until crackling. Third, mix the remaining sauce with fresh hand-pulled noodles — the spicy broth coating every strand is the real finale. Pro tip: the best texture comes from live eels prepared on the spot. If a restaurant doesn't have live eels in the tank, skip it. The dish should taste "fresh-spicy" (鲜辣), not "heavy-spicy" (重辣) — the eel's natural sweetness should come through.
dishes.culturalCode: Why this dish matters beyond taste: Linjiang Eel represents Leshan's unique "fresh-spicy" (鲜辣) tradition, distinct from Chengdu's "numbing-spicy" (麻辣). The use of an ox-bone knife instead of a metal one is a culinary tradition dating back centuries — butchers believed bone doesn't transfer metallic flavors to the eel. The dish also showcases Leshan's rice-paddy ecosystem: eels raised in the same paddies that produce Leshan's famous rice, creating a self-contained culinary cycle.
dishes.honestTalk: The honest truth: Eel can be texturally challenging for first-timers. It's soft, slippery, and has a distinct flavor — some love it immediately, others need a few tries. The crispy fried eel bones are a must-try even if you're squeamish — they taste like seasoned potato chips with a hint of seafood. If the thought of whole eel is too much, ask for the "shredded-only" preparation without the bone course. And this dish is genuinely spicy — not the sneaky kind, but upfront and intense. Have a cold beer ready.

dishes.name: Suji Fried Rice Puff Candy (Mihuatang)
dishes.description: A traditional Leshan sweet snack made from premium glutinous rice, puffed in pork fat and bound with maltose syrup into snowy-white blocks studded with peanuts and sesame. Each bite shatters with a crisp "crunch" that melts into sweet, nutty fragrance — like a Chinese version of crispy rice treats, but lighter and more delicate.
dishes.history: Originally called "Lard Rice Flowers" (猪油谷花), this snack originated in Suji Town, Leshan and dates back to the Ming Dynasty. In 1901 (Guangxu 27th year), artisan Zhang Jiwu perfected the recipe, and it spread to Suji in the early 20th century. Known for being "fragrant, sweet, crispy, and crunchy," it was once exported overseas. In 2009, it was listed in the Sichuan Provincial Intangible Cultural Heritage list — a century-old taste of Leshan childhood.
dishes.method: Follows over 20 traditional steps. Select premium Leshan glutinous rice, soak, steam, and sun-dry to make "yin mi" (阴米). Fry in pork lard until each grain puffs into a white flower. Separately boil white sugar and maltose into syrup, mix with puffed rice, peanuts, and sesame. Press into a mold while warm, cool, and cut into blocks. Entirely handmade, no additives.
dishes.eatingGuide: How to eat it: Best enjoyed in your hand — bite down and listen for the "crunch." The texture should be airy but not crumbly, sweet but not cloying. Traditional way: with a cup of hot tea or coffee — the warmth softens the candy slightly and balances the sweetness. Modern way: crumble it over yogurt or bingfen (ice jelly) for a crunchy topping. Pro tip: fresh-made mihuatang from Suji is noticeably better — the puffed rice is still crisp and the maltose hasn't hardened. Avoid vacuum-packed versions sold in tourist shops; they're often stale.
dishes.culturalCode: Why this dish matters beyond taste: Suji Mihuatang represents the pinnacle of Leshan's snack-making tradition — transforming humble ingredients (rice, lard, sugar) into something extraordinary through pure craftsmanship. The 20+ step process is a dying art; few young artisans are learning it. It's also a window into pre-industrial Chinese confectionery: no machines, no preservatives, just skill and patience. For older Leshan residents, the taste of mihuatang is the taste of childhood — a rare sweet treat in an era of scarcity.
dishes.honestTalk: The honest truth: Mihuatang is very sweet. If you're not used to Chinese-style sweets, a single piece is enough — they're dense with sugar and lard flavor. The pork lard gives it a richness that vegetable oil versions can't replicate, but it also means it's not light. Freshness is everything: if the candy is hard and sticks to your teeth instead of shattering, it's old. The best souvenir is buying it from a small workshop in Suji Ancient Town, not a gift shop. And yes, it will leave crumbs everywhere.

dishes.name: Sweet and Sour Carp
dishes.description: Yellow River carp fried golden with tail raised high, draped in an amber sweet-and-sour sauce. The skin cracks like thin ice; within, the flesh is tender and snow-white. Sour leads into sweet, sweetness never overwhelming freshness, with a glossy glaze clinging to the plate—the definitive taste of New Year in old Jinan memory.
dishes.history: Rooted in traditional Yellow River carp cookery, Jinan's Huiquan Lou famously fried live carp to order in the late Qing. Shandong sweet-sour technique demands 'fry first, then glaze.' The dish crystallized in the Republican era as the signature of Yanxi Tang and Jufeng De, witnessing Jinan's port-city banquet splendor.
dishes.method:
Score carp in peony-cut pattern, marinate with salt and Shaoxing wine 15 min
Coat with starch batter, hold tail, lower into 70% hot oil; fry until set, then re-fry for crispness
Separately stir-fry scallion, ginger, garlic; make sauce with sugar-to-vinegar 2:1
Thicken with wet starch, add hot oil to brighten and bubble the glaze
Pour sauce over fish immediately and serve sizzling hot

dishes.name: Braised Intestines in Nine Turns
dishes.description: Intestines pass through blanching, boiling, layering, and braising; the result is date-red, glossy, shaped in looping coils. Texture is soft-sticky yet springy: first sour, then sweet, then salty, finishing with light bitterness and spice—five flavors rotating on the tongue in rich sauce, revealing the true meaning of 'nine turns'.
dishes.history: In the Guangxu era of Qing, Manager Du of Jinan's Jiuhua Lou, who loved intestines, created this dish. Named from the Daodejing's 'Nine-Turn Golden Elixir'—the process as intricate as refining immortality pills. Later refined by Lu cuisine masters, it became famed north-south as official cuisine; during the Republic, Peking opera stars always ordered it when visiting Ji'nan.
dishes.method:
Rub pork intestines with salt and vinegar to remove odor; blanch, then boil with scallion and ginger until 80% cooked
Layer intestines (two or three tubes nested) for thickness; cut into sections
Stir-fry over medium heat until both sides turn golden and slightly charred
Add Shaoxing wine, soy sauce, sugar, clear stock, amomum powder, cinnamon powder; simmer 20 min over low heat
Reduce over high heat, drizzle with Sichuan pepper oil, flip, and plate in chrysanthemum shape

dishes.name: Cattail Shoots in Milk Broth
dishes.description: Tender hearts of Daming Lake cattail shoots simmered in milk-white broth, thick and mellow as fresh cream. Shoots are translucent, crisp, and fiber-free, with a clean sweetness that echoes. The soup tastes rich yet light, lifted by ham and shiitake—one spoonful seems to drink the essence of a spring itself, a unique vegetarian treasure of the spring city.
dishes.history: Cattail shoots rank among Jinan's 'Three Beauties' (with lotus root and water caltrop). Records of eating bulrush shoots appear in the Northern Wei's Qimin Yaoshu. Qing-era Jinan milk broth, made from hen, pork hock, and duck carcass, met cattail shoots to become an official banquet classic, perfected at Jinsheng Lou, with literati praising it 'clear as autumn dew.'
dishes.method:
Remove hard husk from cattail shoots; take tender core and slice; shred ham, shiitake, and bamboo shoots
Simmer hen, pork hock, and duck bones at least 3 hours; strain for pure stock
Bring stock to boil; add shoots, ham, shiitake; simmer 2 min over low heat
Season with salt, Shaoxing wine, ginger juice; no soy sauce to keep soup white
Finish with chicken fat or lard; ladle into bowl, scatter pea shoots on top

dishes.name: Poached Sea Clam in Supreme Chicken Broth
dishes.description: A masterpiece of Fuzhou cuisine, this dish highlights the ultimate freshness of the sea. Plump, translucent sea clams are briefly blanched in a crystal-clear, intensely flavorful chicken broth. The meat is remarkably tender and sweet, while the broth is rich yet refreshing, embodying the Fuzhou culinary philosophy of preserving the original taste of premium ingredients.
dishes.history: Originating from Changle District in Fuzhou, the specific sea clam used is the 'Zhanggang Sea Clam,' renowned for its unique sweetness and crisp texture. In the 1980s, this dish was served at state banquets, cementing its status as a crown jewel of Min cuisine. The technique of 'quick-boiling' requires impeccable timing, reflecting the high culinary standards of Fuzhou chefs.
dishes.method:
1. Prepare the supreme chicken broth by simmering old hen, pork ribs, and premium ham for hours, then clarify it with minced chicken breast to achieve a crystal-clear appearance.
2. Carefully shuck the fresh Zhanggang sea clams, remove the internal organs, and gently wash them without damaging the delicate meat.
3. Slice the clam meat into thin, even pieces to ensure uniform cooking and optimal texture.
4. Bring a pot of water to a rapid boil, briefly blanch the clam slices for merely 10 to 15 seconds until they slightly curl and turn opaque.
5. Immediately transfer the blanched clams into a pre-heated serving bowl.
6. Pour the boiling hot, crystal-clear chicken broth over the clams, seasoning with a pinch of salt and white pepper to finish.

dishes.name: Lychee-Shaped Sweet and Sour Pork
dishes.description: A classic Fuzhou dish that showcases both culinary artistry and a delightful flavor profile. Pork is scored with a precise cross-hatch pattern, deep-fried to curl into the shape of a lychee fruit, and then tossed in a vibrant sweet and sour sauce. The result is a dish that is crispy on the outside, tender on the inside, and bursting with a tangy, fruity aroma.
dishes.history: Dating back to the Qing Dynasty, Lychee Pork is a testament to the ingenuity of Fuzhou chefs. Since fresh lychees were rare in northern Fuzhou, local cooks used their exceptional knife skills to transform ordinary pork into the shape of the beloved tropical fruit. The dish has been passed down for centuries, remaining a staple at festive banquets and family gatherings in Fujian.
dishes.method:
1. Select lean pork tenderloin, score it with a fine cross-hatch pattern on one side, and cut it into bite-sized pieces, ensuring the cuts are deep enough to curl when fried.
2. Marinate the pork pieces with light soy sauce, rice wine, and a touch of red yeast rice powder for color.
3. Coat the marinated pork evenly with sweet potato starch, pressing gently so the starch adheres to the scored crevices.
4. Deep-fry the pork in hot oil until it curls into the shape of a lychee and turns golden and crispy, then remove and drain.
5. Prepare the sweet and sour sauce by simmering sugar, black vinegar, tomato paste, soy sauce, and a little water in a wok until slightly thickened.
6. Toss the fried pork and blanched water chestnuts in the sauce quickly over high heat, ensuring every piece is evenly coated, and serve immediately.

dishes.name: Drunken Chicken with Red Wine Lees
dishes.description: A signature cold dish that highlights Fuzhou's unique obsession with 'Zao' (red fermented rice lees). Tender poached chicken is marinated in a fragrant mixture of red wine lees, rice wine, and spices. The meat absorbs the deep, ruby-red color and a complex, intoxicating aroma of fermented rice, offering a savory, slightly sweet, and profoundly umami flavor.
dishes.history: The use of red wine lees is a defining characteristic of Fuzhou cuisine, dating back over a thousand years to the Tang and Song dynasties. Red lees, made by fermenting rice with Monascus purpureus yeast, were historically used to preserve food and add a unique flavor. Drunken Red-Lees Chicken evolved from this ancient preservation technique into a celebrated delicacy, symbolizing the coastal people's ingenuity in flavor creation.
dishes.method:
1. Poach a whole free-range chicken in a gently simmering broth of ginger, scallions, and Shaoxing wine until just cooked through, then immediately plunge it into ice water to tighten the skin and retain juiciness.
2. Chop the cooled chicken into neat, bite-sized pieces with the bone in.
3. In a bowl, thoroughly mix premium Fuzhou red wine lees with rice wine, salt, sugar, and a pinch of MSG to create a smooth, aromatic marinade.
4. Place the chicken pieces in a deep container and evenly coat them with the red lees mixture, ensuring every piece is fully submerged in the marinade.
5. Seal the container and refrigerate for at least 6 to 8 hours, allowing the meat to absorb the vibrant red color and the intoxicating lees fragrance.
6. Arrange the marinated chicken on a serving plate, garnish with a sprinkle of toasted sesame or fresh coriander, and serve chilled.

dishes.name: Cao Cao Chicken
dishes.description: A legendary medicinal braised chicken from Hefei, infused with a blend of traditional Chinese herbs. The meat is tender, the skin is glossy, and the flavor is rich with a subtle herbal aroma, reflecting the harmony of culinary and medical arts.
dishes.history: Legend has it that during the Three Kingdoms period, Cao Cao suffered from severe headaches while stationed in Luzhou (modern-day Hefei). A local physician prescribed a chicken stewed with Chinese herbs, which remarkably alleviated his symptoms. The dish was later named in his honor and has been passed down for over a thousand years.
dishes.method:
1. Clean a whole free-range chicken and blanch it in boiling water with ginger and scallions to remove impurities.
2. Prepare a spice bag with over a dozen traditional Chinese herbs, including astragalus, angelica root, and goji berries.
3. Create a rich master stock using soy sauce, rock sugar, Shaoxing wine, and the herb bag.
4. Simmer the chicken in the master stock over low heat for about an hour until fully cooked and infused.
5. Remove the chicken, brush its skin with sesame oil, and let it rest to absorb the flavors.
6. Chop the chicken into pieces, arrange on a plate, and drizzle with the reduced, thickened herbal broth.

dishes.name: Lord Bao's Fish
dishes.description: A signature Hefei dish featuring fish braised until the bones are completely soft and edible. Coated in a dark, glossy sauce, it offers a complex flavor profile of savory, sweet, and slight tanginess, symbolizing the incorruptible spirit of Lord Bao Zheng.
dishes.history: Named after Bao Zheng, a famous and incorruptible judge of the Song Dynasty who was born in Hefei. The locals created this dish using black fish and lotus root, cooking it until the bones melt in the mouth to symbolize Bao's unyielding integrity and 'iron bones.' It remains a staple at local banquets.
dishes.method:
1. Score a cleaned crucian carp or black fish, coat it lightly in starch, and deep-fry until the exterior is crispy and golden.
2. In a separate wok, caramelize rock sugar and add ginger, scallions, star anise, and dark soy sauce to build the sauce base.
3. Pour in Shaoxing wine and a splash of black vinegar, then add enough water to submerge the fish.
4. Place the fried fish and lotus root slices into the wok, bringing the liquid to a boil.
5. Cover and simmer on the lowest heat for over two hours until the bones are entirely tender.
6. Reduce the sauce over high heat until thick and glossy, then carefully transfer the fish to a plate.

dishes.name: Wushan Tribute Goose
dishes.description: Originating from Wushan Town in Hefei, this premium braised goose is renowned for its succulent meat and fragrant, complex marinade. The skin is a rich amber, and the meat is tender yet chewy, carrying a deep umami flavor that has delighted emperors and commoners alike.
dishes.history: Dating back to the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, the local ruler of Luzhou presented a specially braised goose to the emperor as a tribute. The emperor was highly impressed by its exceptional taste, decreeing it an annual royal tribute. The recipe has been meticulously preserved in Wushan Town ever since.
dishes.method:
1. Select a plump, free-range goose, clean it thoroughly, and blanch it in boiling water to tighten the skin.
2. Prepare a proprietary spice blend featuring sand ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, and dried tangerine peel.
3. Sauté the spices and aromatics in oil, then add rock sugar, premium soy sauce, and a rich bone broth.
4. Submerge the goose in the fragrant master brine, ensuring it is fully covered, and bring to a gentle boil.
5. Turn off the heat and let the goose steep in the residual warmth of the brine for several hours to deeply absorb the flavors.
6. Remove the goose, chop it into uniform pieces, and serve with a ladle of the warm, aromatic brine.

dishes.name: Steamed Wuchang Fish
dishes.description: A quintessential Hubei dish featuring the Wuchang bream, celebrated for its tender, sweet meat and delicate flavor. The fish is simply steamed with ginger, scallions, and a light soy-based dressing to highlight its natural freshness, embodying the culinary philosophy of preserving the original taste of premium river ingredients.
dishes.history: The fame of this dish skyrocketed in 1965 when Chairman Mao Zedong wrote the famous poem 'Swimming', which included the line 'I have just drunk the water of Changsha, and now I am eating the Wuchang fish.' Since then, it has transcended a mere local delicacy to become a cultural icon of Wuhan, frequently served at state banquets and high-end gatherings.
dishes.method:
1. Select a live Wuchang bream, scale it, clean the cavity, and score both sides of the fish with shallow diagonal cuts.
2. Rub the fish lightly with salt and Shaoxing wine, then stuff the cavity and the cuts with julienned ginger and scallion segments to marinate for 15 minutes.
3. Place the fish on a heat-proof plate, arranging chopsticks underneath to allow steam to circulate evenly, and steam over vigorously boiling water for exactly 8 to 10 minutes.
4. Remove the plate, carefully discard the melted juices and the old ginger and scallions, as they carry the fishy odor.
5. Garnish generously with fresh julienned ginger, scallion threads, and red chili strips, then drizzle with hot smoking oil to release their aromas.
6. Finally, pour a specially prepared mixture of steamed fish soy sauce and a touch of sugar around the edges of the plate before serving.

dishes.name: Pork Ribs and Lotus Root Soup
dishes.description: The ultimate comfort food in Wuhan, this rich, slow-simmered soup features pork ribs and the region's prized lotus roots. The lotus roots, specifically cultivated in the muddy wetlands of Hubei, become remarkably starchy, soft, and slightly sweet after hours of braising, while the broth turns a beautiful milky pink and absorbs the deep savory essence of the pork.
dishes.history: Hubei is known as the 'Hometown of Lotus Roots,' and the tradition of brewing soup in earthenware pots dates back over a thousand years to the Chu State period. In Wuhan, no family reunion or holiday feast is complete without a pot of rib and lotus root soup. The local earthenware pot, called a 'Diaozi,' is essential for achieving the soup's signature thick and mellow texture, representing the deep-rooted culinary heritage of the Chu people.
dishes.method:
1. Choose high-starchy lotus roots from local wetlands, peel them, and cut them into large, thick chunks; soak them in water to prevent oxidation.
2. Blanch the pork ribs in cold water with ginger and cooking wine, then rinse thoroughly to remove impurities and blood scum.
3. Place the ribs, lotus root chunks, and a few slices of ginger into a traditional Hubei earthenware pot, adding enough cold water to submerge all ingredients.
4. Bring to a boil over high heat, skim off any remaining foam, then reduce to a very low simmer and cover tightly.
5. Simmer gently for at least 2 to 3 hours until the lotus roots are perfectly starchy and the broth turns a rich, creamy pinkish-white.
6. Season with salt and white pepper just before turning off the heat, and garnish with freshly chopped cilantro and scallions.

dishes.name: Stir-fried Hongshan Purple Cabbage with Cured Pork
dishes.description: A legendary seasonal delicacy exclusive to Wuhan, this dish pairs the crisp, sweet, and slightly peppery Hongshan purple cabbage with rich, smoky cured pork. The cabbage, grown in the unique microclimate of the Hongshan district, possesses a vibrant purple hue and a tender texture that perfectly balances the savory, salty fat of the winter-cured pork.
dishes.history: The Hongshan purple cabbage has been a tribute to the imperial court since the Song Dynasty, celebrated for its unique taste that cannot be replicated outside its native soil. The famous Qing Dynasty poet and food enthusiast Yuan Mei praised its exceptional quality in his culinary writings. Paired with traditional cured pork, this dish became a staple of high-end Wuhan banquets during the late Qing and early Republican eras, symbolizing the pinnacle of winter dining in the region.
dishes.method:
1. Select fresh Hongshan purple cabbages, snap the stems to remove the tough outer skin, and break them into uniform 4-centimeter segments by hand for a better texture.
2. Slice the winter-cured pork belly into thin, even pieces, and blanch them briefly in boiling water to remove excess salt and surface impurities.
3. Heat a wok, add a small amount of oil, and render the pork slices over medium-low heat until the fat becomes translucent and slightly crispy.
4. Toss in minced ginger, garlic, and dried chili segments, stir-frying briefly to release their fragrant oils into the rendered pork fat.
5. Increase the heat to high, add the cabbage stems first and stir-fry for a minute, then add the leaves, splashing a little Shaoxing wine around the wok edges.
6. Stir-fry rapidly until the cabbage is just tender but still crisp, season lightly with sugar to balance the saltiness, and serve immediately.

dishes.name: Stir-fried Cured Pork with Artemisia Grass
dishes.description: In Nanchang, there is a saying: 'The grass of Poyang Lake is the treasure of Nanchang people.' Artemisia grass is a unique wild aquatic plant from the Poyang Lake area, carrying a distinct, refreshing fragrance. When stir-fried with homemade cured pork smoked over cypress branches, the rich fat of the pork permeates the grass, while the grass's aroma cuts through the greasiness. The dish boasts a golden hue and a crisp, tender texture, offering a savory taste filled with the essence of spring, perfectly embodying the 'authentic and original flavors' of Gan cuisine.
dishes.history: This dish originated from the daily lives of fishermen along Poyang Lake. Legend has it that during the Ming Dynasty, when Zhu Yuanzhang and Chen Youliang fought a fierce battle on the lake, military rations were scarce. Fishermen fed the troops with wild artemisia grass from the lake and their own cured pork, accidentally discovering the exquisite combination. Artemisia grass was documented in the 'Nanchang County Annals' during the Qing Dynasty. By the Republic of China era, it had become a signature dish in Nanchang restaurants and is now one of the most representative dishes of Gan cuisine nationwide.
dishes.method:
1. Trim the tough roots of the fresh artemisia grass, wash it thoroughly, and cut it into inch-long sections; wash the cured pork to remove surface soot, then slice it thinly.
2. Add a little oil to the wok, put in the pork slices, and stir-fry over medium-low heat until the pork renders its fat and the edges curl slightly, turning golden brown.
3. Scoop out the excess rendered lard, leaving just a little oil in the wok; add shredded ginger and dried red chili segments to stir-fry until fragrant.
4. Turn to high heat, quickly add the prepared artemisia grass, and stir-fry evenly so that the grass is well-coated with the pork fat.
5. Splash a little cooking wine around the edge of the wok to enhance the aroma, add a dash of light soy sauce for umami; since the cured pork is already salty, no extra salt is usually needed.
6. Stir-fry until the grass is just cooked but remains crisp, add a pinch of chicken bouillon, drizzle with a few drops of sesame oil, toss well, and serve immediately.

dishes.name: Nanchang Three-Cup Chicken
dishes.description: Nanchang Three-Cup Chicken is a classic poultry dish in Gan cuisine. Unlike its Taiwanese counterpart, the Nanchang version does not use Thai basil and adds not a single drop of water. Its essence lies in the 'three cups': one cup of tea oil (or lard), one cup of brewed rice wine, and one cup of premium soy sauce. The chicken is slow-braised in a sealed clay pot with these three ingredients. The result is a vibrant red dish with tender meat, where the wine and soy sauce aromas intertwine perfectly. It is rich, mellow, and not greasy, showcasing Nanchang people's ultimate pursuit of heat control and seasoning.
dishes.history: Legend traces back to the late Southern Song Dynasty when Wen Tianxiang, a national hero, was captured by the Yuan army. Nanchang locals went to visit him. A jailer brought chicken, rice wine, and soy sauce, but due to poor conditions, he braised the chicken with one cup of rice wine, one cup of soy sauce, and one cup of tea oil (or lard) as a tribute. After Wen's martyrdom, the dish spread among the people. Although not directly recorded in Yuan Mei's 'Suiyuan Shidan' in the Qing Dynasty, the 'three-cup' cooking method has existed in Nanchang folk cuisine for hundreds of years, serving as the signature dish of time-honored local restaurants.
dishes.method:
1. Select a tender yellow-feathered chicken, clean it, chop it into bite-sized pieces, soak in cold water to remove blood, then drain and set aside.
2. Line the bottom of a clay pot with scallion sections and ginger slices to prevent sticking and add base aroma; spread the drained chicken pieces evenly over the aromatics.
3. Pour in one cup of tea oil (or lard), one cup of local Nanchang brewed rice wine, and one cup of premium soy sauce, ensuring the liquid covers about two-thirds of the chicken.
4. Cover the clay pot, bring the broth to a boil over high heat first, then reduce to a very low simmer, sealing it to braise for about 30 to 40 minutes.
5. Do not open the lid during the process, allowing the chicken to fully absorb the flavors through the steam and boiling of the 'three cups' until the sauce thickens and the chicken becomes tender.
6. Uncover and turn to high heat to reduce the sauce; once the thick, glossy sauce coats the chicken, remove the scallions and ginger, drizzle with a little finishing oil for shine, and serve directly in the pot.

dishes.name: Nanchang Earthen Jar Slow-Simmered Soup
dishes.description: 'A bowl of earthen jar soup is half the history of Nanchang.' This soup is the soul of Nanchang people's breakfast and daily diet. It uses specially made giant earthen jars as containers, with numerous small jars placed inside, simmered over hard charcoal for hours. No complex spices are added; it relies solely on the natural flavors of the ingredients and water, achieving a clear, non-greasy, thick but not oily, and richly savory taste. The minced pork patty soup is the most classic variant, where the meat aroma perfectly blends with the original juice, warming both the stomach and the heart.
dishes.history: The history of earthen jar soup can be traced back to the Northern Song Dynasty, reportedly related to the construction of Nanchang's Tengwang Pavilion. To replenish their energy during hard labor, workers placed ingredients in earthen jars and roasted them over fires, accidentally discovering the exceptionally delicious broth. The 'Nanchang Prefecture Annals' of the Qing Dynasty documented the folk practice of simmering soup in earthen jars. In modern times, 'earthen jar soup shops' in the streets and alleys of Nanchang have become a unique urban landscape, and in 2011, the making technique of Nanchang earthen jar soup was listed as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Jiangxi Province.
dishes.method:
1. Select pork front leg meat with a good ratio of lean to fat; mince it finely by hand, add a little minced ginger, chopped scallions, salt, and a pinch of white pepper, and stir in one direction until it becomes sticky and well-combined.
2. Place the seasoned minced meat at the bottom of a small earthen jar, press it firmly with a spoon to form an even patty, and poke a few small holes in the center with chopsticks to allow the broth to seep in.
3. Add an appropriate amount of clean water above the patty, filling the jar to about 80%; add two drops of cooking wine to remove any gamey odor, strictly avoiding artificial flavor enhancers like MSG.
4. Cover the small earthen jars and arrange them neatly on the middle iron rack inside the specially made giant earthen jar.
5. Light hard charcoal at the bottom of the giant jar, control the heat, and simmer at a constant low temperature for 4 to 6 hours, allowing the nutrients and umami of the ingredients to fully release into the soup.
6. After simmering, use a dedicated iron hook to take out the small jar, uncover it to reveal a clear broth with a rich meat aroma, sprinkle with a little chopped scallion, and it is ready to be consumed directly.
